parsed.narrative: mr. caesar came betimes to teach the boy, and he spoke with him seriously about what he would do if the boy did not look after his lute and singing. he said that if the boy did not attend to them, he would turn him away, and he hoped this would do some good upon the boy. all the morning he was busy at the office, dined at home at noon, and returned to the office very busy till very late before going home to supper and bed. later, he wrote that his wife was making great preparation to go to Court to Chappell the next day, and he received news from Mr. Coventry that the fleet had sailed from Harwich to the coast of Holland. on the lord’s day, he took his wife and her woman to White Hall Chappell, heard Stillingfleete preach, was mightily treated at Mr. Povy’s, took the air in the fields beyond St. Pancras, and after supper had arguments about a corant before all parted friends.

He then heard a mean sorry sermon of Mr. Mills, went to the Dolphin Taverne, and dined with the officers of the navy and the commissioners of the ordnance, with good musique at his direction. canon.summary: he went out betimes in a fine frost and walked to Redriffe, then called and drank at Half-way house, hoping to overtake some of the women of the house but could not. in london he visited his wife, was a little displeased at her being so forward to make much of her brother and sister, but all ended well presently, and he afterward cleared his money matters to his complete satisfaction. he later dined merrily with sir w. warren and others, came home by water to greenwich with the river beginning to be full of ice, and was a little frighted but got home well. at night he had little mrs. tooker, mrs. daniel, and sarah to his chamber to cards and sup, and mr. pierce told him that w. howe had been examined and had used his name about sending goods, which vexed him mightily, though he did not speak much of it then. after more cards he broke up late, having great pleasure with his little girle, mrs. tooker.

canon.subject: accounts
canon.summary: at the office all the morning, then at noon dined at captain cocke’s with the company, and though the meat was good, being all frost-bitten it was most of it unroast. the afternoon was pleasant, and after leaving them he went back to the office, wrote his letters, and went home with his head full of business and some trouble for letting his accounts go so far. that night he made an oath not to drink wine till he had passed his accounts and cleared all. coming home, he had supper with a woman provided by the boy’s sister daniel, and after supper they were alone a great while. he also says mrs. burrows, an old acquaintance and a most pretty woman, came to him that day, and he had a kiss or two of her.

parsed.narrative: he spent the morning considering instructions for signing and paying bills, and then read them publicly with sir j. minnes and sir w. batten. at noon mr. hill came to town with mr. houbland, and he left his lord and dinner to dine with them, saying he was glad to see them. after dinner he was called away by mr. andrews, and by a fine glosse brought him to desire tallys for tangier victuals, clearing to himself l210 and noting his late profits. later he spent the evening with lord bruncker, who opened and made up his watch, which pleased him, though he was vexed by a snappish answer from madam williams and concluded by a letter from the lord duke of albemarle pressing meetings through christmas. he ended by making up his journal, easing his mind, and noting the frosty weather and hope for an abatement of the plague, though he feared it would continue next year if it did not.

parsed.narrative: the weather hath been frosty these eight or nine days, and so he and others hope for an abatement of the plague the next weeke. otherwise he says the plague will certainly continue the next year. through the day he was occupied with instructions about signing bills, dinner with mr. hill and mr. houbland, and later with mr. andrews about tangier victualls. in the evening he was pleased by seeing lord bruncker take his watch to pieces and make it up again, and he notes that his mind was eased when he made up his journall for 8 or 9 days. he closes by linking the frost and the plague, and by saying he is concluded in continuing meetings for all christmas and must make often visits to the lord duke after he has evened his accounts.
